title: Doughnut economics

definition.text: A doughnut-shaped picture of sustainable development that joins planetary boundaries (an outer ecological ceiling) with a social foundation of basic human needs (an inner ring).

facts.text: The hole in the middle shows people lacking life's essentials such as healthcare and education; the outer crust shows the ecological ceilings that must not be overshot.
Economist Kate Raworth developed it in a 2012 Oxfam paper and expanded it in her 2017 book Doughnut Economics.
An economy counts as prosperous when all twelve social foundations are met without overshooting any of the nine ecological ceilings, leaving a 'safe and just space for humanity'.
The social foundations draw on the UN Sustainable Development Goals; the ecological ceilings come from the planetary boundaries of Rockström and Steffen's group.
A 2018 study of 150 countries found none that met its citizens' basic needs while keeping resource use at a globally sustainable level.
Raworth says significant GDP growth is still needed for low- and middle-income countries to reach the social foundation.
Critics say it lacks empirical support; one formal test found higher economic freedom linked with less imbalance, not more.
Branko Milanović notes that bringing everyone to rich countries' median income would require world GDP to triple, which the model does not address.

contested_note: Economists dispute whether the model has empirical support and whether it fairly represents mainstream economics.

title: Eco-economic decoupling

definition.text: The idea that an economy could grow without a matching rise in pressure on the environment.

facts.text: In many economies rising production (GDP) increases environmental pressure; a decoupled economy would keep growing while using less water, fossil fuel and other resources.
It is often measured by the emission intensity of economic output, meaning pollution per unit of GDP.
In 2002 the OECD defined decoupling as breaking the link between 'environmental bads' and 'economic goods'.
Where decoupling has occurred, one proposed explanation is the shift to a service economy; the environmental Kuznets curve is a proposed model of it.

The UNEP International Resource Panel warned in 2011 that without decoupling humanity could use 140 billion tons of minerals, ores, fossil fuels and biomass a year by 2050, three times the then-current rate.
Its 2016 report found global material productivity had declined since about 2000, so the world economy needed more materials per unit of GDP, the opposite sometimes called overcoupling.
Proposed technologies to speed decoupling include energy-saving, metal- and mineral-saving, and freshwater- and biotic-resource-saving technologies.

contested_note: Whether, how far and how fast growth can be decoupled from environmental pressure is widely debated.

definition.text: Relative decoupling means environmental impact per unit of output falls while total impact may still rise; absolute decoupling means total impact falls while output grows.

facts.text: For absolute decoupling, resource efficiency must rise at least as fast as economic output and keep improving as the economy grows.
Under relative decoupling total environmental impacts still increase, only more slowly than GDP.
Tim Jackson found much evidence of relative decoupling in the global economy but said evidence for absolute decoupling is harder to find.
Between 1990 and 2015 carbon intensity per dollar of GDP fell 0.6% a year while population and income per person each grew 1.3% a year, so emissions rose about 2% a year.
Herman Daly noted that a dollar of GNP in 1969 used half the materials of a dollar in 1900, yet total material consumption rose 400 percent.

title: Five axes of decoupling
article: Eco-economic decoupling#Five axes to assess decoupling

definition.text: A set of at least five dimensions for judging whether a claimed case of decoupling is real and enough.

facts.text: Overall decoupling covers all environmental indicators, partial decoupling only some, which matters when cutting emissions raises, say, mining.
Local decoupling may simply move environmental stress to other countries by outsourcing production, unlike global decoupling.
Decoupling can be temporary if growth and pressures re-couple later; to be sufficient it must be large and fast enough to stay clear of critical tipping points.

definition.text: Resource decoupling cuts the resources used per unit of economic activity; impact decoupling cuts the environmental harm caused while output grows.

facts.text: Resource decoupling is also called dematerialization: using less material, energy, water and land for the same economic activity.
The impacts targeted by impact decoupling arise from extracting resources.

title: Decoupling evidence debate
article: Eco-economic decoupling#Lack of evidence for decoupling

definition.text: The dispute over whether growth has been, or can be, decoupled from environmental pressure fast enough to avoid serious damage.

facts.text: A 2020 study found no evidence of economy-wide decoupling nationally or internationally, and studies found absolute decoupling rare.
Critics say there is no evidence of decoupling near the needed scale and that a sufficiency approach must complement efficiency.
Hickel and Kallis's models assume carbon intensity falls at most 4% a year, which makes 1.5 °C impossible and 2 °C reachable only if rich economies shrink by over 90%.
Rikard Warlenius replies that absolute decoupling faster than that 4% threshold has already happened and stronger policies could push it higher.
He also argues growth is better placed than degrowth to fund the deep, costly transitions the IPCC describes.

contested_note: Degrowth scholars see no evidence of sufficient decoupling, while others point to cases of fast absolute decoupling and argue stronger policy could achieve more.
